### Delhi District Court
## Ms. Asiya Jamil vs The Canara Bank on 8 April, 2009
IN THE COURT OF SH. BALWANT RAI BANSAL: ARC: CENTRAL:
TIS HAZARI COURTS: DELHI
Ms. Asiya Jamil
D/o Late Sh. Jamil­Ur­Rehman
R/o 2237, Naya Mohalla,
Qasim Jaan Street,
Ballimaran,
Delhi­110 006
...... Petitioner
Versus
The Canara Bank
635, Gandhi Katra
Delhi­110 006
Through its Branch Manager
also at:
2378­82, Chashma Building
Ballimaran
Delhi­110 006
...... Respondent
Eviction Petition u/s 14 (1) (b) and (f) of cite8†Delhi Rent Control Act
Date of Institution of the case           :   24.02.2007
Date of Judgment reserved                 :   23.03.2009
Date of Judgment pronounced               :   08.04.2009
JUDGMENT:

1. The present petition is an eviction petition filed on the grounds u/s 14 (1) (b) and (f) of cite8†Delhi Rent Control Act against the respondent in respect of one godown on the ground floor of the suit property bearing no. 2378­82, Chasma Building, Ballimaran, Delhi ­ 6.

2. Brief facts, as stated in the petition, are that the petitioner is the owner and landlady of the suit property and same has been let out to M/s Lakshmi Commercial Bank Ltd. @ Rs.240/­ p.m. but M/s Lakshmi Commercial Bank Ltd. is later on claimed to have been merged and was taken over by the present respondent bank and with this merger/acquisition the existence of M/s Lakshmi Commercial Bank Ltd.

has been brought to an end which amounts to sub­letting, assigning or parting with the possession of the suit premises without the consent of the petitioner. It is stated that the suit property has been lying locked for the last about 14 years and due to its closure for a long time, substantial damage has been caused or permitted to have been caused to the suit property.

It is further stated that the suit property has been rendered collapsible any moment and is an alive danger for the other occupants of this property as well passers by and therefore immediate repairs to the premises is required which is not possible unless vacant possession thereof is handed over to the petitioner. It has been prayed that an eviction order may be passed in favour of the petitioner and against the respondent in respect of suit premises.

3. The respondent bank has contested the present petition ­ 3 ­ and filed the written statement in which it has been submitted that in exercise of powers conferred under sub section (4) of cite9†Section 45 of the Banking Regulation Act 1949, Reserve Bank of India prepared a scheme for amalgamation of the Lakshmi Commercial Bank Ltd.

with Canara Bank and the said scheme sanctioned by the Central Government under cite10†Section 45 (7) of the said Act and was notified in the gazette of India dated 23.08.1985 and the said amalgamation is not a transfer of tenancy and does not amount to an act of sub­letting, assignment or parting with the premises and therefore present petition is not maintainable on the ground of sub­letting cite11†u/s 14 (1) (b) of DRC Act and is liable to be dismissed.
It has been contended that petitioner has thorough knowledge that the premises in suit has been continuously in occupation of the respondent since the amalgamation of M/s Lakshmi Commercial Bank Ltd.

with Canara Bank as the petitioner has been continuously residing in the same locality/area where the premises in suit is situated and the petitioner and her representative have been regularly visiting the premises in suit and have never raised any objection to the premises being occupied by the respondent as a tenant.

It has been submitted that the respondent bank has been in exclusive possession of tenanted premises since last 22 years in its own capacity and therefore there has been a implied consent of the landlord/petitioner for creation of tenancy in favour of the respondent. It is further contended that the petitioner was maintaining a saving account along with Mst. Atiya Rehman in their joint names with the respondent bank at Chandni Chowk Branch and the rent @ Rs.

240/­ per month has been credited in to the said Saving Account of the petitioner and the said rent was withdrawn from time to time by the petitioner and as such by her ­ 4 ­ conduct , the petitioner had impliedly accepted the respondent as her tenant and it cannot be alleged at this stage after the gap of 22 years by the landlord/ petitioner that the respondent bank is a sub­tenant in the tenanted premises.

It has been further contended that there is no cause of action on the ground u/s 14 (1) (f) of cite8†DRC Act and it has been submitted that the tenanted premises are being used as a godown by the respondent bank which is opened regularly by the bank officials and the same do not require any substantial repairs and are not in a dangerous condition and moreover no such document has been filed by the petitioner to show that she had applied to Local Authority for getting the Plans sanctioned or that the Local Authority had issued any notice to the petitioner to carry out repairs on account of unsafe condition of the premises or that she has necessary funds for reconstruction.

It has been further contended that present eviction petition filed by the petitioner is time barred as the petitioner/landlord did not take any action for years against the respondent bank and therefore the tenancy rights accrued in favour of the respondent. It has been further contended that the petitioner only wants to evict the respondent as she wants to let out the tenanted premise at a higher price and the respondent being the old tenant is an hurdle for the same.
The respondent has prayed for dismissal of the petition.
4. The petitioner has filed the replication in which the averments made in the petition are reiterated and the averments made in the written statement are stated to be wrong and controverted.

5. In order to prove her case the petitioner has examined ­ 5 ­ herself as PW­1 and evidence by way of affidavit has been filed as Ex. P­1 in which she has reiterated the averments made in the petition. She has placed on record the site plan as Ex. PW­1/1, the newspaper clipping alognwith its translation as Ex. PW­1/2 (Colly) and certified copy of permission from Competent Authority (Slum) as Ex. PW­1/3.

6. On the other hand, the respondent bank has examined Sh. R.K. Gupta, Sr. Manager, Canara Bank as RW­1 and evidence by way of affidavit has been filed as Ex.R1/A in which averments made in the written statement has been reiterated. He has placed on record the Notification of Government of India dated 23.08.1985 published in Gazette of India as Ex. RW­1/1, certified copy of the Statement of Account of saving account of the petitioner as Ex.
RW­1/2 (Colly) and letter dated 13.05.04 by the petitioner to the respondent bank with regard to change of her address as Ex. RW­1/3 and Ex. RW­1/4.
7. I have heard the counsel for the parties and perused the record carefully.

8. Ground U/s 14(1)(b) of cite8†DRC Act 14 (1) (b) of cite8†DRC Act reads as under:­ That the tenant has on or after the 9th day of 1952 sub let, assigned or otherwise parted with the possession of the whole or any part of the premises without obtaining the consent in writing of the landlord.

9. The Ld, Counsel for the petitioner has argued that the petitioner had let out the suit premises to M/s Lakshmi ­ 6 ­ Commercial Bank Ltd. and M/s Lakshmi Commercial Bank Ltd. is claimed to have been merged and taken over by the respondent and as such M/s Lakshmi Commercial Bank Ltd. ceased to exist and this merger/acquisition has been done without the consent of the petitioner and therefore it amounts to subletting, assigning or parting with the possession of the suit premises. The Ld.

Counsel for the petitioner has relied upon in support of his contentions the authorities titled as Parasam H. Rao Vs. Shantiprassad N. Kumar 1980 cite12†RLR SC 747, Cox & Kings Ltd. Vs. Chander Malhotra 1997 RLR 116 (SC), South Asia Industries Pvt. Ltd. Vs. S. Anup Singh and cite13†Singer India Ltd., Appellant Vs. Chander Mohan Chadha & Ors , Respondents AIR 2004 SC 4368.

10. On the other hand the Ld. Counsel for the respondent has vehemently argued that under the scheme of amalgamation u/s (4) of cite9†Section 45 of Banking Regulation Act 1949, RBI prepared a scheme for amalgamation of M/s Lakshmi Commercial Bank Ltd. with the Canara Bank which was sanctioned by the Central Government and the same was notified in the Gazette of India dated 23.08.1985 and as such M/s Lakshmi Commercial Bank Ltd.

merged with the Canara Bank under the legislative scheme and therefore it does not amount to subletting, assigning or parting with the possession of the suit premises. Ld. Counsel for the respondent has vehemently contended that the respondent is not sub tenant under the petitioner as the M/s Lakshmi Commercial Bank Ltd.

was merged with the Canara Bank in the year 1985 and the present petition has been filed after a gap of 22 years and moreover, the respondent bank has been paying the rent all along to the petitioner and the petitioner was also maintaining a saving ­ 7 ­ account with the Canara Bank since 1988. She has further argued that the petitioner knows that the respondent bank has taken over M/s Lakshmi Commercial Bank Ltd.

and the respondent bank is also remitting the rentals in the account of the petitioner and petitioner has not raised any objections for the last 22 years and therefore by virtue of acquiescence, the respondent has become the tenant as the petitioner has by her conduct accepted the respondent as a tenant. The Ld.

Counsel for the respondent has also argued that by virtue of aforesaid merger, all the assets and liabilities including the lease agreement, movable and immovable properties were taken over by the Canara Bank . In support of her contention, the Ld. Counsel for the respondent has relied upon in an authority titled as "cite14†Mrs. Asha Rohtagi & Ors. Vs Erstwhile New Bank of India through General Manager PNB". On the other hand, Ld.

Counsel for the petitioner has argued that the authority relied upon by the Ld. Counsel for the respondent is not applicable in the facts and circumstances of the present case as the management of M/s Lakshmi Commercial Bank Ltd. which was the tenant of the petitioner and the management of the Canara Bank are entirely different and in the authority relied upon by Ld. Counsel for the respondent, both the banks were Nationalised bank.

11. Facts in the present case are within the narrow compass. The case of the petitioner is that M/s Lakshmi Commercial Bank Ltd. was the tenant and same has been merged with the Canara Bank without the consent of the petitioner and it amounts to subletting, assigning or parting with the possession of the suit premises. On the other hand, the stand of the respondent bank is ­ 8 ­ that M/s Lakshmi Commercial Bank Ltd.

has been merged with the Canara Bank under the legislative scheme by virtue of notification sanctioned by the Central Government cite15†u/s 45 (7) of Banking Regulation Act 1949 on 23.08.1985 and amalgamation under the legislative scheme does not amount to subletting, assigning or parting with the possession of the suit premises.

12. Admittedly, M/s Lakshmi Commercial Bank Ltd. was the tenant of the petitioner and the same has been merged with the Canara Bank by virtue of a scheme prepared by the Reserve Bank of India for amalgamation of Lakshmi Commercial Bank Ltd. with the Canara Bank in exercise of powers conferred under sub­ section (4) of cite9†Section 45 of Banking Regulation Act 1949 .

13. Now, it has to be seen whether the aforesaid amalgamation/merger of the M/s Lakshmi Commercial Bank Ltd. with the Canara Bank amounts to subletting, assigning or parting with the possession of the suit premises. The respondent has proved the notification issued by the Govt. of India, Ministry of Finance, Department of Economic Affairs (Banking Division), New Delhi, dated 23.08.1985 as Ex.

RW­1/1 and as per notification, RBI in exercise of powers conferred under sub section (4) of cite9†Section 45 of Banking Regulation Act 1949 has prepared a scheme for amalgamation of M/s Lakshmi Commercial Bank Ltd. with the Canara Bank and in exercise of of powers conferred under cite10†Section 45 (7) of the said Act, the Central Government has sanctioned the scheme of amalgamation as per terms and conditions mentioned in the notification Ex. RW­1/1. The relevant part i.e. clause (2) of notification Ex.
RW­1/1 reads as under:

> "As from the date which the Central Government may specify for ­ 9 ­ this purpose under sub­section (7) of cite10†Section 45 of the said Act (hereinafter referred to as the prescribed date) all rights, powers, claims, demands, interests, authorities, privileges, benefits, assets and properties of the transferor bank, movable and immovable, including premises subject to all incidents of tenure and to the rents and other sums of money and covenants reserved by or contained in the leases or agreements under which they are held, all office, furniture, loose equipment, plant, apparatus and appliances, books, papers, stocks of stationery, other stocks and stores, all investments in stocks, shares and securities, all bills receivable in hand and in transit, all cash in hand and on current or deposit account (including money at call or short notice) with banks, bullion, all book debts, mortgage debts and other debts with the benefit of securities, or any guarantee therefor, all other, if any, property rights and assets benefit of all guarantees in connection with the business of the transferor bank shall, subject to the other provisions of this scheme, stand transferred to, and become the properties and assets of, the transferee bank; and as from the prescribed date all the liabilities, duties and obligations of the transferor bank shall be and shall become the liabilities, duties and obligations of the transferee bank to the extent and in the manner provided hereinafter."
14. I have gone through the authorities relied upon by both the Ld. counsels for the parties.

15. In the authorities relied upon by Ld. Counsel for the petitioner, the tenant somehow was found to be instrumental in bringing about the amalgamation and transfer of tenancy rights. However, in the present case, the amalgamation of M/s Lakshmi ­ 10 ­ Commercial Bank Ltd. with the Canara Bank is an act of legislation. The facts in the authority "cite14†Mrs. Asha Rohtagi & Ors. Vs Erstwhile New Bank of India through General Manager PNB"
> relied upon by the Ld. Counsel for the respondent are similar to the facts in the present case.

In the aforesaid authority, the New Bank of India was merged with the Punjab National Bank vide notification dated 04.09.1993 issued by Government of India cite16†u/s 9 of the Banking Companies Act 1980 and the question arose whether the aforesaid amalgamation/merger amounts to subletting, assigning or parting with the possession of the demised premise and it was held in the aforesaid authority that this scheme was legislative in character and it does not amount to subletting, assigning or parting with the possession of the demised premises.

In the aforesaid authority, the Hon'b le High Court of Delhi also referred and discussed all the authorities relied upon by the Ld. Counsel for the petitioner and it was held that the in all those cases, the tenant some how was found to be instrumental in bringing about the amalgamation and transfer of tenancy rights.

It was also held that the tenancy rights have been conferred on the Punjab National Bank by statute namely clause 4(2) of the notification dated 04.09.1993 promulgated by Central Government under cite16†Section 9 of the Banking Companies Act. 1980 which scheme is legislative in character. It does not amount to merger of two companies under the provisions of cite17†Companies Act . Therefore the ratio of M/s Parasram Harnand Rao, M/s cite12†General Radio and Appliances Co. Ltd and others and Cox & Kings Ltd.
and another Vs. Chandler Malhotra will not apply to the facts of the present case.

16. Similarly the facts of the present case are squarely covered with the facts in the authority "cite14†Mrs. Asha Rohtagi & Ors. Vs Erstwhile New Bank of India through General Manager PNB" . As discussed herein above, it was held by the Hon'b le High Court of Delhi that amalgamation is an act of legislation and same does not amount to subletting, assigning or parting with the possession of the demised premises.

In the present case also, the tenancy rights have been conferred on the Canara Bank by statute namely clause 2 of the notification dated 23.08.1985 promulgated by Central Government under Sub Section (4) of cite9†Section 45 of the Banking Regulation Act 1949. A perusal of clause 2 of notification Ex.

RW­1/1 shows that all rights, powers, claims, demands, interests, authorities, privileges, benefits, assets and properties of the transferor bank, movable and immovable, including premises subject to all incidents of tenure and to the rent and other sums of money and covenants reserved by or contained in the leases or agreements under which they are held stand transferred to the transferee bank. Thus the tenancy rights of the M/s Lakshmi Commercial Bank Ltd.

have been conferred to Canara Bank by clause 2 of notification dated 23.08.1985 issued under Sub Section (4) of cite9†Section 45 of the Banking Regulation Act 1949 and it does not amount to sub­letting, assigning or parting with the possession of the suit premises.

17. In view of aforesaid discussions and categorical law cite14†laid down by the Hon'b le High Court of Delhi in "cite14†Mrs. Asha Rohtagi & Ors. Vs Erstwhile New Bank of India through General Manager PNB", in the present case also the acquisition/merger of M/s Lakshmi Commercial Bank Ltd. with Canara Bank does not ­ 12 ­ amount to sub­letting, assigning or parting with the possession of the suit premises as the merger/acquisition has been done under the legislative scheme. So far the contention of the Ld.

Counsel for the petitioner that the management of M/s Lakshmi Commercial Bank Ltd. and management of Canara Bank are different and therefore the law cite14†laid down by Hon'b le High Court of Delhi is not applicable in the present case, is without any merit. It makes hardly any difference that management of two banks is not the same as the scheme by virtue of which M/s Lakshmi Commercial Bank Ltd.

has been merged into the Canara Bank is legislative in nature and therefore in view of law cite14†laid down by the Hon'b le High Court of Delhi it does not amount to sub­letting, assigning or parting with the possession of the suit premises.

18. I also find considerable force in the contention of the Ld. Counsel for the respondent that by way of her conduct the petitioner has impliedly accepted the respondent as a tenant. In the present case, admittedly the rentals of the tenanted premises is paid by the respondent bank to the petitioner. Admittedly, the petitioner has opened a saving account with the respondent bank in the year 1988 and the account opening form dated 04.07.08 is Ex. PW­1/R­1.

Admittedly, the suit property is situated within the premises where the petitioner is residing. PW­1 has also admitted in her cross­examination that she has known about the merger of Laxmi Commercial Bank Ltd. for the last 15­16 years. The aforesaid statement of PW­1 shows that the petitioner is in the knowledge of existence of Canara Bank for the last 15­16 years.

She is also maintaining a saving account with the respondent bank and she is also receiving rent from the respondent bank and she has never raised any objections to the occupation of the ­ 13 ­ respondent bank in the suit premises. This shows that the petitioner has acquiesced the respondent as a tenant.

19. In view of aforesaid discussion, in my considered opinion, the petitioner has failed to prove that the merger/acquisition of M/s Lakshmi Commercial Bank Ltd. with the Canara Bank amounts to sub­letting, assigning or parting with the possession of the suit premises. Therefore, no ground is made out cite11†u/s 14 (1) (b) of DRC Act and present petition is dismissed under this ground.

20. Ground U/s 14(1)(f) of cite8†DRC Act That the premises have become unsafe or unfit for human habitation and are required bonafide by the landlord for carrying out repairs which cannot be carried out out without the premises being vacated.

21. The case of the petitioner is that the suit premises has been lying locked for the last about 14 years and due to its closure for a long time, substantial damage has been caused to the suit property and the suit property has been rendered collapsible any moment and same requires immediate repairs which is not possible unless the vacant possession is handed over to the petitioner.

On the other hand, the respondent has denied that the suit premises remains lying locked and it has been contended that the the suit premises are being used as a godown by the respondent bank which is opened regularly by the bank official and same is not in a dangerous condition and does not require any repairs.

22. The onus was upon the petitioner to lead cogent evidence to prove that the suit premises have become unfit and unsafe for dwelling and it has become dangerous and collapsible at any moment and same requires immediate repairs, but the petitioner has failed to lead any cogent evidence to prove the aforesaid ground. The petitioner has not examined any expert witness or architect to prove that what damage has been caused to the suit property and to prove that suit premises requires immediate repairs.

Even the petitioner has failed to place on record the photographs showing extent of damage and condition of building. Although, the petitioner has placed on record the newspaper clipping Ex. PW­1/2 (Colly) to prove that the suit property which is also known as Chasma Building has become dangerous but merely by filing the newspaper cutting, the grounds u/s 14 (1) (f) of cite8†DRC Act is not proved. Ld.

Counsel for the petitioner has argued that premises in question was built in 1950' s and it has outlived its age as the premises are 60 years old and are unfit and unsafe for human habitation. In support of his contention he has relied upon in "cite18†Jagdish & Another Vs. Sanjay Kumar & Ors.," Punjab & Haryana High Court. I do not find any merit in this contention of the Ld.
Counsel for the petitioner for the want of insufficient evidence to prove that suit premises have become unfit and unsafe for human habitation. The facts in the authority relied upon by the Ld.

Counsel for the petitioner is not applicable in the present case as in the authority there was ample evidence that the suit shop has become unfit and unsafe for human habitation and it has developed cracks and same has become dangerous but in the present case there is no evidence regarding the condition of the suit property as discussed herein ­ 15 ­ above. The petitioner has not led any cogent and clinching evidence regarding the existing condition of the suit property.
Therefore, the petitioner has failed to prove the grounds cite19†u/s 14 (1)
(f) of cite8†DRC Act and thus the petition is dismissed under this ground also.
23. In view of aforesaid discussions, the present petition cite11†u/s 14 (1) (b) and cite20†u/s 14 (1) (f) of Delhi Rent Control Act is dismissed. No order as to costs.
File be consigned to Record Room.
Announced in the open court                           (Balwant Rai Bansal)
on 8th April, 2009                                   ARC, Central, Delhi

### Delhi District Court
## R/O Flat No:9 vs National Insurance Co. Ltd. Division No on 28 November, 2011
IN THE COURT OF ADDITIONAL RENT CONTROLLER, PATIALA
HOUSE COURTS, NEW DELHI
Raghunandan SaranAshok Saran (HUF),
40­42, Janpath, New Delhi,
through its Karta Ashok Saran
R/o flat No:9, 40­42, Janpath, New Delhi           .....Petitioner
Versus
1. National Insurance Co. Ltd. Division No:1,
4, Peareylal Bldg, 42­Janpath, New Delhi­110001
2. Sh. M.L. Sharma  S/o Kundan Lal
R/o 40­42, Janpath, New Delhi­110001
3. Roop Sharma S/o M.L. Sharma
R/o 40­42, Janpath, New Delhi­110001
4. Rajiv Nanda S/o Om Prakash Nanda,
R/o 40­42, Janpath, New Delhi­110001
PETITION UNDER SECTION 14(1)(B) OF DELHI RENT CONTROL
DATE OF INSTITUTION OF THE PETITION
EC No:E­13/08/09, Raghunandan Saran Ashok Saran (HUF)  Vs. National
Insurance Co. Ltd.
DATE OF FINAL ARGUMENT/CLARIFICATION
DATE OF FINAL JUDGMENT
JUDGMENT

1. Petitioner has filed the present petition u/s 14(1)(b) of Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 against the respondents for eviction from the tenanted premises comprises of Second Floor, Flat No:2, bearing Municipal No:
> 40/6, of premises on third floor bearing Municipal No:40/16 and of premises on Second Floor, Flat No:3, bearing Municipal No:40/7 ( Portion of 40­42, Janpath, New Delhi).

2. It is stated by the petitioner that he is the landlord of the aforesaid premises and National Insurance Co. Ltd. is the tenant regarding aforesaid premises. It is averred by the petitioner that originally premises were leased to New Zealand Insurance Co. Ltd. w.e.f. 1940 which company subsequently was nationalized by Government of India and subsumed under National Insurance Company Limited.

It is further averred by the petitioner that total rate of rent regarding tenanted premises since 1940 is Rs.283/­ It is stated by the petitioner that portion of the suit premises has been and is in exclusive possession of Sh. M.L Sharma , Roop Sharma and Rajiv Handa being given without written consent of the landlord.
EC No:E­13/08/09, Raghunandan Saran Ashok Saran (HUF) Vs. National Insurance Co. Ltd.

3. Petitioner stated that he has sought eviction of tenant on the ground that tenant has sublet, assigned or otherwise parted with possession of a part of the premises, without obtaining the consent in writing of the landlord, to one M. L. Sharma, to one Roop Sharma and to one Rajiv Handa who have been and are in exclusive possession of portion of the premises bearing Municipal No:40/16.

4. Written statement filed on behalf of the respondent No:1. It is denied by the defendant No:1 that portion of the suit premises has been in exclusive possession of M.L.Sharma, Roop Sharma and Rajiv Handa. It is further stated that Defendant No:1 has absolutely no concerned with the aforesaid persons.

Defendant No:1 further denied that they have sublet, assigned or otherwise parted with the possession of a part of premises without obtaining the consent in writing of landlord to M.L.Sharma, Roop Sharma and Rajiv Handa who have been and are in exclusive possession of portion of premises bearing No:40/16. Defendant No:1 stated that he is in possession of the premises in its entirely and the portion of subletting etc. does not arise at all.
Defendant No:1 prayed for dismissal of the petition of the petitioner with costs.

5. Defendant No:2 to 4 have also filed their written statement. It is stated that plaintiff has not come to the court with clean hands and EC No:E­13/08/09, Raghunandan Saran Ashok Saran (HUF) Vs. National Insurance Co. Ltd.

suppressed material facts as it is very much in the knowledge of the petitioner that respondent No:2 was in the employment of the Respondent No:1 since 1952 and therefore, the respondent No:2 was provided with the accommodation situated at 3rd Floor of property No:40/16, Pyare Lal Building, Janpath, New Delhi.

It is submitted that previously the company was deducting the amount on account of provision of the premises from the salary of the respondent No:2 but later on with the change of management, the company stopped deducting any amount from the salary of the respondent No:2 and treated as free accommodation and even after the retirement of the respondent No:2 in 1978 the company never asked for the vacation of the premises in dispute from the respondent and since then the respondent No:2 is residing there and there is no question of subletting to him.

It is denied by the defendants No:2 to 4 that portion of the premises was given to the them without any written consent of the landlord. It is stated that respondent No:3 Roop sharma is the con of the respondent No:2 and Sh. Rajeev Nanda­respondent No:4 is the son­in­law of the respondent No:2 and they are not staying permanently in the suit premises and they being the close relative of the respondent No:2 frequently visiting the respondent No:2, otherwise said Sh. Roop Sharma and Sh.
Rajeev Nanda have nothing to do with the EC No:E­13/08/09, Raghunandan Saran Ashok Saran (HUF) Vs. National Insurance Co. Ltd.
premises in question.

6. Petitioner Ashok Saran filed his evidence by way of affidavit which is Ex. P­1 bearing his signature at point A and B and reiterated the contents of his main petition. Site plan showing the various portions of property bearing No:40­40, Janpath, New Delhi , comprising suit premises is Ex. PW1/1. Notice u/o XII rule 4 cite8†CPC dt.22­2­2006 sent to respondent No:1 through Registered A/D is Ex. PW1/2, its A/D card is Ex. PW1/3.

Another notice under order XII rule 8 cite8†CPC r/w cite9†section 66 of Indian Evidence Act dt.31­8­2001 is Ex.PW1/4 and its A/D card and its copy is Ex. PW1/5 & Ex. PW1/6, postal receipt is Ex. PW1/7. Photocopy of the MTNL telephone Director 1999 Volume II Page 1704 is Ex. PW1/9.

During his cross examination by the ld. Counsel for the respondent No:1, PW1 Ashok Saran stated that he can not say whether any lease deed or written document was executed when the property in question was let out. PW1 stated that he was not the Karta of the petitioner in 1940 when the tenancy was created and even he was not present at the time of creation of tenancy. He further stated that he is not aware whether any written agreement for tenancy was executed or not.
PW1 stated that 40/6,40/7 and 40/16 are located in Piare Lal Building built on two plots EC No:E­13/08/09, Raghunandan Saran Ashok Saran (HUF) Vs. National Insurance Co. Ltd.

bearing No:40 & 42. PW1 denied the suggestion that second floor is not a part of the premises No:40/16 as shown in blue colour in the site plan Ex. PW1/1. PW1 admitted that flat No:2 and 3 are being used for residential purposes. PW1 voluntarily deposed that it was used for residential purposes only after petition u/s 14(1)(k) of cite10†DRC Act were initiated and user was changed from commercial to residential and only second floor portion was used for office of New Zealand Insurance Company.

PW1 stated that portion shown in blue colour in Ex. PW1/1 was always used for residential purposes but he is not aware of the fact that who was in the possession of blue portion in 1972. PW2 stated that he does not know respondent No:2 personally and whether he has been retired from New Zealand Insurance Company. PW1 denied the suggestion that there is no subletting or parting with the possession by respondent No:1.
PW1 further denied that Ex.PW1/8 and PW1/9 does not indicate as to the respondent No:2 is in possession of which portion of property No:40/16.
No other witness has been examined by the petitioner and petitioner closed his evidence on 24­05­2008.

7. Respondent No:1 examined Sh. Ram Niwas, Deputy manager, National Insurance Co. Ltd as RW1 and filed his evidence by way of EC No:E­13/08/09, Raghunandan Saran Ashok Saran (HUF) Vs. National Insurance Co. Ltd.

affidavit which is Ex. R1W­1/A. It is deposed by R1W1 Sh. Ram Niwas that tenanted premises was let out by the petitioner to M/s New Zealand Insurance Co Ltd. In 1940 which company stood transferred to and vested in the respondent No:1 company copy vide notification dt.1­1­1973 is Ex. R1. R1W1 Sh. Ram Niwas. R1W1 Sh.

Ram Niwas deposed that respondent No:2 was in the employment of the said M/s New Zealand Insurance Company and on account of his employment with the said company, he was permitted user of a portion of the said property by the said company even before 1972. R1W1 Sh. Ram Niwas deposed that defendant No:1 has never sublet, assigned or otherwise parted with possession of any portion of the tenanted premises to defendant No:2 to 8 or to any other person.

R1W1 Sh. Ram Niwas was cross examined by the petitioner at length. During his cross examination R1W1 Sh. Ram Niwas stated that he never worked in New Zealand Insurance Company and paragraph No:1 of his affidavit is on the basis of personal knowledge and remaining paragraphs no:2 to 9 are based on the office record. R1W1 Sh. Ram Niwas stated that he was not present when the premises was taken on rent and also when Respondent No:2 got his employment with the New Zealand Insurance Co.
During the cross examination of R1W1 Sh. Ram EC No:E­13/08/09, Raghunandan Saran Ashok Saran (HUF) Vs. National Insurance Co. Ltd.

Niwas, attendance register and leave register of the respondent No:1 w.e.f. 1976 to 1979, filed on behalf of the respondent No:1 has been marked as R­1 , running on page 209 to page 667. R1W1 Sh. Ram Niwas admitted that name of Sh. M.L. Sharma is not mentioned in the list mark R­1. He further stated that he has no personal knowledge in respect of employment of Sh. M.L. Sharma.

8. I have heard the Karta of petitioner and ld. Counsel for the respondent at length and given my thoughtful consideration to the entire records and evidence led by both the parties.

9. The petitioner­herein is seeking eviction of the premises on the basis of subletting on part of the R­1 i.e. The National Insurance Co. to the Respondents No. 2 to 4. The R­1 has stated that the company has been in the EC No:E­13/08/09, Raghunandan Saran Ashok Saran (HUF) Vs. National Insurance Co. Ltd.

11. The Respondents No.2 to 4 have filed a joint reply and have averred that the respondent R­2 had been in the employment of one Newzealand Insurance Company. the year 1952. It was in course of the said employment that the R­2 was provided an accommodation on the third floor of the premises. The previous company i.e. the Newzealand Insurance co.

used to deduct the accommodation­rent from his salary. However, when the National Insurance Co. stepped into the shoe of the previous company, no accommodation­rent was deducted. 12.WHETHER THE PETITIONER ­HUF HAS HAS PROPERLY INSTITUTED BY ITS KARTA ?

The respondent R­1 has raised the objection that the petitioner is not an HUF. In that regard the petitioner was cross­examined whether the petitioner had filed any document to show that Raghunandan Saran Ashok Saran was constituted as an HUF. To the said question the petitioner EC No:E­13/08/09, Raghunandan Saran Ashok Saran (HUF) Vs. National Insurance Co. Ltd.

replied that he had not filed any document but the HUF status of the family stood admitted by the respondents. When the petitioner was asked whether he can furnish details thereof, the petitioner stated that at present his wife Madhulika Saran, his son Nonny, his unmarried daughter Alika Saran and his daughter­in­law are the members of the HUF apart from him. It was admitted by the petitioner that he was not the Karta in the year 1940 when the tenancy was created.

A Hindu Undivided Family as is understood under the law consists of at least a co­parcenery. A co­parcenary consist of descendants from a common ancestor up­to the four degree and any property which is acquired by co­parceners through common ascendant is a HUF property or any property which is added to the property of HUF by a co­parcener and any business which is being carried on by such co­parceners together is a business of HUF.
In the present case there is nothing on record to show that the tenancy was created by an HUF.

In Sunil Kumar and another Vs. Ram Prakash and others [supra], this court held as follows: ­ "In a Hindu family, the Karta or Manager occupies a unique position. It is not as if anybody could become Manager of a joint Hindu family. As a general rule, the father of a family, if alive, and in EC No:E­13/08/09, Raghunandan Saran Ashok Saran (HUF) Vs. National Insurance Co. Ltd.
his absence the senior member of the family, is alone entitled to manage the joint family property."

The above made observations were interpreted by the Honble Supreme Court in M/s cite11†Nopany Investments (P) Ltd v Santokh Singh (HUF ) ­ Case No.: Appeal (civil) 5761 of 2007 ­ Bench: Tarun Chatterjee & P.Sathasivam (10th Dec 2007):

> "From a reading of the aforesaid observation of this court in Sunil Kumar and another Vs. Ram Prakash and others [supra], we are unable to accept that a younger brother of a Joint Hindu Family would not at all be entitled to manage the joint family property as the Karta of the family. This decision only lays down a general rule that the father of a family, if alive, and in his absence the senior member of the family would be entitled to manage the joint family property."

In the present there seems to be no protest by any member of the joint hindu family to the filing of the present petition suit by the petitioner­herein claiming himself to be the Karta of the HUF. The petitioner was never put any suggestion to the effect that the family was undivided or that there was any other person more competent to maintain the present proceedings. Another decision which comes to the rescue of EC No:E­13/08/09, Raghunandan Saran Ashok Saran (HUF) Vs. National Insurance Co. Ltd.

the petitioner­herein is cite12†Narendrakumar J. Modi Vs. Commissioner of Income Tax, Gujarat II, Ahmedabad [(AIR) 1976 SC 1953], wherein it was held that so long as the members of a family remain undivided, the senior member of the family is entitled to manage the family properties and is presumed to be manager until contrary is shown. In the present case no suggestion has been put by the respondents which could show the contrary.

13.WHETHER THE CASE UNDER cite13†S.14(1)(b) IS MAINITANABLE (YES) In the instant case though there is no written tenancy document, the relationship of landlord and tenant has not been denied by the respondents No.1 to 4.

Before adverting to the contentions raised at the Bar, it will be convenient to reproduce cite13†Section 14(1)(b) of the Act,which reads as under :­ "14. Protection of tenant against eviction.­ (1) Notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in any other law or contract, no order or decree for the recovery of possession of any premises shall be made by any Court or Controller in favour of the landlord against a tenant :
> Provided that the Controller may, on an application made to him in EC No:E­13/08/09, Raghunandan Saran Ashok Saran (HUF) Vs. National Insurance Co. Ltd.
> the prescribed manner, make an order for the recovery of possession of the premises on one or more of the following grounds only, namely­

> (b) that the tenant has, on or after the 9th day of June, 1952 sub­let, assigned or otherwise parted with the possession of the whole or any part of the premises without obtaining the consent in writing of the landlord............"

There is no ambiguity in the Section and it clearly says that if, without obtaining the consent in writing of the landlord the tenant has, on or after 9­6­1952, a. sub­let, or b. assigned, or c. otherwise parted with the possession of the whole or any part of the premises, the tenant would be liable for eviction.

A plain reading of this provision would show that if a tenant has sublet or assigned or otherwise parted with the possession of the whole or any part of the premises without obtaining the consent in writing of the landlord, he would be liable to be evicted from the said premises. That is to say, the following ingredients must be satisfied before an order of EC No:E­13/08/09, Raghunandan Saran Ashok Saran (HUF) Vs. National Insurance Co. Ltd.
eviction can be passed on the ground of subletting :­ d. The tenant has sublet or assigned or parted with the possession of the whole or any part of the premises;
e. Such subletting or assigning or parting with the possession has been done without obtaining the consent in writing of the landlord.
The language of cite13†S.14 (b) is wide enough not only to include any sub­lease but even an assignment or any other mode by which possession of the tenanted premises is parted.

The applicability of the Section depends upon occurrence of a factual situation, namely, sub­letting or assignment or otherwise parting with possession of the whole or any part of the premises by the tenant.

The respondent R­1 has specifically raised the issue of involuntariness on its part and has contended that involuntary action such as the merging of the previous company into the present company in lieu of the notification dated 01.01.1973 would not attract the provision of cite14†S.14(1)(b) of the DRC Act,1958. In that regard there are several judgments which says that it is irrelevant whether the act is voluntary on part of the tenant and the EC No:E­13/08/09, Raghunandan Saran Ashok Saran (HUF) Vs.
National Insurance Co. Ltd.

reasons for doing so are wholly irrelevant and can have no bearing. This view finds support from an earlier decision rendered in M/s. Parasram Harnand Rao v. M/s. Shanti Prasad Narinder Kumar Jain and another, AIR 1980 SC 1655, wherein it was held that the language of cite15†Section 14(1)

(b) is wide enough not only to include any sub­lease but even an assignment or any other mode by which possession of the tenanted premises is parted and the provision does not exclude even an involuntary sale.

It was held by a three judge bench in "cite16†Singer India Ltd. v. Chander Mohan Chadha "(AIR 2004 SC 4368) that even under an amalgamation scheme where the leases, rights of tenancy or occupancy of the Transferor Company get vested in and become the property of the Transferee Company, it would make no difference insofar as the applicability of cite14†S. 14(1)(b) is concerned, as the Act does not make any exception in favour of a lessee who may have adopted such a course of action.

In the said case, the landlord had filed an eviction petition on the ground that the tenant, an American Company, without obtaining any written consent from the landlord, had parted with the possession of the premises in dispute in favour of Indian Company Limited and it was the said company which was in exclusive possession of the premises and EC No:E­13/08/09, Raghunandan Saran Ashok Saran (HUF) Vs. National Insurance Co. Ltd.

thereby it was liable for eviction in view of cite14†S. 14(1)(b) of the Act. Under the scheme of amalgamation that whole of the business, property, undertaking, assets, including leases, rights of tenancy, occupancy etc. stood transferred to and vested in the Indian Company.
In Halsbury's Laws of England (4th Edn.), para 1539, the attributes of amalgamation of companies have been stated as under :

> "Amalgamation is a blending of two or more existing undertakings into one undertaking, the shareholders of each blending company becoming substantially the shareholders in the company which is to carry on the blended undertakings. There may be amalgamation either by the transfer of two or more undertakings to a new company, or by the transfer of one or more undertakings to an existing company.

Strictly "amalgamation" does not, it seems, cover the mere acquisition by a company of the share capital of other companies which remain in existence and continue their undertakings, but the context to which the term is used may show that it is intended to include such an acquisition."

In cite17†Saraswati Industrial Undertaking v. CIT, Haryana , AIR 1991 SC 70 (para 6), it has been held that there can be no doubt that when two EC No:E­13/08/09, Raghunandan Saran Ashok Saran (HUF) Vs. National Insurance Co. Ltd.

companies amalgamate and merge into one, the Transferor Company loses its identity as it ceases to have its business. However, their respective rights or liabilities are determined under the scheme of amalgamation, but the corporate identity of the Transferor Company ceases to exist with effect from the date of amalgamation is made effective. Therefore, in view of the settled legal position, the original lessee i.e. the Newzealand Insurance Co.
ceased to exist with effect from the Appointed Day and thereafter the R­1 came in possession and is in occupation of the premises in dispute.

The effect of parting of possession of the tenanted premises as a result of scheme of amalgamation of companies has also been considered in two other decisions. In M/s. cite18†General Radio and Appliances Co. Ltd. and others v. M. A. Khader , 1986 (2) SCC 656, which is a decision by a Bench of three learned Judges, the premises had been let out to M/s. General Radio and Appliances Co. Ltd.

On account of a scheme of amalgamation sanctioned by the High Court under cite19†Sections 391 and cite20†394 of the Companies Act, all property, rights and powers of every description including tenancy right, held by M/s. General Radio and Appliances Co. Ltd. had been blended with M/s. National Ekco Radio and Engineering Co. Ltd. Thereafter the landlord instituted proceedings for eviction on the EC No:E­13/08/09, Raghunandan Saran Ashok Saran (HUF) Vs. National Insurance Co. Ltd.

ground of unauthorized sub­letting. It was urged on behalf of the original tenant that the amalgamation of M/s. General Radio and Appliances Co. Ltd. (appellant No. 1) with M/s. National Ekco Radio and Engineering Co. Ltd.) was an involuntary one which had been brought into being on the basis of the order passed by the High Court under cite19†Sections 391 and cite20†394 of the Companies Act and that the appellant No.

1 Company had not been wound up and/or liquidated, but had been merely blended with appellant No. 2 on the basis of the order of the Court and consequently there was no sub­letting by appellant No. 1 Company to appellant No. 2 Company. It was also urged that appellant No. 1 Company had not become extinct but had been merged and/or blended with appellant No. 2 Company.

It was held that under the relevant Act, there was no express provision that in case of any involuntary transfer or transfer of the tenancy right by virtue of a scheme of amalgamation sanctioned by the High Court by its order under cite19†Sections 391 and cite20†394 of the Companies Act, such a transfer will not come within the purview of cite21†Section 10(ii)(a) of Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act. On this finding, it was held that the appellant was liable for eviction.

cite22†Cox and Kings Ltd. and another v. Chander Malhotra , 1997 (2) SCC 687 is also a decision by a Bench of three learned Judges and arose EC No:E­13/08/09, Raghunandan Saran Ashok Saran (HUF) Vs. National Insurance Co. Ltd.

out of proceedings for eviction under cite14†Section 14(1)(b) of Delhi Rent Control Act. Here, the premises were given on lease to Cox and Kings (AGENTS) Limited, a company incorporated under the United Kingdom Companies Act (for short, "Foreign Company"). A petition for eviction was filed on several grounds and one of the grounds was of sub­letting to Cox and Kings Limited, a company registered under the cite23†Indian Companies Act (for short an "Indian Company").

It was contended on behalf of the appellant that in view of cite24†Section 29 of FERA, the Foreign Company was required to obtain written permission from the Reserve Bank of India to carry on business. The said permission was sought for but was refused.

As a consequence, the Indian Company, namely, Cox and Kings Limited was floated in which the Foreign Company sought to have 100 per cent shares, but on refusal of permission had only 40 per cent of shares in the business to which approval was given by the Reserve Bank of India. Thereafter, the Indian Company carried on business in the same premises.

It was urged that as the transfer of leasehold interest from the Foreign Company to the Indian Company was by compulsion, it was an involuntary one and, therefore, it was not a case of sub­letting within the meaning of cite25†Section 14(1)(b) of the Act. It was held that under FERA, there was no compulsion that the premises demised to the Foreign EC No:E­13/08/09, Raghunandan Saran Ashok Saran (HUF) Vs. National Insurance Co. Ltd.

Company should be continued or given to the Indian Company. On the other hand, under the agreement executed between the Foreign Company and the Indian Company, incidental to the assignment of the business as a growing concern, the Foreign Company also assigned the monthly and other tenancies and all rented premises of the assignor in India to the Indian Company.

The Court, accordingly, concluded that though by operation of FERA the Foreign Company had wound up its business, but under the agreement it had assigned the leasehold interest in the demised premises to the Indian Company which was carrying on the same business in the tenanted premises without obtaining the written consent of the landlord and, therefore, it was a clear case of sub­letting. After referring to the earlier decisions in M/s. Parasram Harnand Rao v. M/s.

Shanti Prasad Narinder Kumar Jain (supra) and M/s. cite18†General Radio and Appliances Co. Ltd. v. M. A. Khader (supra), the Court ruled that it was a case of assignment by the Foreign Company to the Indian Company which amounted to sub­letting within the meaning of cite25†Section 14(1)(b) of the Act and the decree for eviction was affirmed.

These cases clearly hold that even if there is a scheme of amalgamation where­under the leases, rights of tenancy or occupancy of the Transferor Company get vested in and become the property of the EC No:E­13/08/09, Raghunandan Saran Ashok Saran (HUF) Vs. National Insurance Co. Ltd.

Transferee Company, it would make no difference insofar as the applicability of cite25†Section 14(1)(b) is concerned, as the Act does not make any exception in favour of a lessee who may have adopted such a course of action.

14.WHETHER THE PARTING OF POSSESSION INFERED FROM OTHER FACTS: (YES) It is well settled that the burden of proving subletting is on the landlord but if the landlord proves that the sub­tenant is in exclusive possession of the suit premises, then the onus is shifted to the tenant to prove that it was not a case of subletting. In the present case the petitioner has cross­examined Sh. Ram Niwas Deputy Manager at length has been able to establish that the name of Sh. M. L.
Sharma was not mentioned in the list of the employees of R­1. Only the employment of R­2 was established.

The petitioner cross­examined Sh. Dinesh Kumar Sharma at great length. The said R­2 admitted that he was never the employee of The Newzealand Insurance Co. He futher admitted that only Sh. M.L.Sharma was the employee of the Newzealand Insurnace Co. and it him alone who was permitted / entitled to stay in the premises as an EC No:E­13/08/09, Raghunandan Saran Ashok Saran (HUF) Vs. National Insurance Co. Ltd.
employee. He further deposed that he did not know of any other employee of the National Insurance Co. who had resided in the premises after the retirement.

The petitioner has also cross­examine Mrs. Madhu Sharma (RW­3) who is the daughter of Sh. M.L.Sharma. She deposed that her father retired and did not work after the year 1980. Sh also admitted that her father has died in the impugned premises. She further deposed that her husband Sh. Rajive Nanda using name Rajive Sharma had never resided in the premises i.e. 40­42 Janpath.

In the present case the factum of the parting of possession can be culled out from the collateral facts which become essential for the purpose of the present case. The respondents R­1 to R­4 have all deposed coherently that the accommodation of R­2 was free of charge when the National Insurance Co. stepped in. The witnesses RW­1 and RW­2 have deposed that an accommodation rent was charged by the previous company and that the National Insurance Co. i.e. R­1 made it absolutely free.

Surprisingly even when R­2 retired from the service no vacating proceedings were initiated against him. The said segment of fact confirms the version of the petitioner­landlord that the possession of the portion of the premises was systematically parted with. Eventually the possession EC No:E­13/08/09, Raghunandan Saran Ashok Saran (HUF) Vs. National Insurance Co. Ltd.
was made exclusive to R­2. The version of the R­1 is silent on the possession of R­3 and R­4.

It is well­settled that parting with possession meant giving possession to persons other than those to whom possession had been given by the lease and the parting with possession must have been by the tenant. User by other person is not parting with possession so long as the tenant retains the legal possession himself, or in other words, there must be vesting of possession by the tenant in another person by divesting himself not only of physical possession but also of the right of possession.

In the present case the respondent R­1 not only parted with the physical possession but also parted with the legal possession by not providing free accommodation and then showing no intention to recover the possession after the retirement. The intention to recover the possession was still missing when the concerned respondent died.

In this regard, it would be sufficient to take note of judgment in the case of cite26†Bharat Sales Ltd. Vs. LIC Of India , (1998) 3 SCC 1, wherein it has been observed:­ "Sub­tenancy or sub­letting comes into existence when the tenant gives up possession of the tenanted accommodation, wholly or in part, and puts another person in exclusive possession thereof. This EC No:E­13/08/09, Raghunandan Saran Ashok Saran (HUF) Vs. National Insurance Co. Ltd.

arrangement comes about obviously under a mutual agreement or understanding between the tenant and the person to whom the possession is so delivered. In this process, the landlord is kept out of the scene.

Rather, the scene is enacted behind the back of the landlord, concealing the overt acts and transferring possession clandestinely to a person who is an utter stranger to the landlord, in the sense that the landlord had not let out the premises to that person nor had he allowed or consented to his entering into possession over the demised property.

It is the actual, physical and exclusive possession of that person, instead of the tenant, which ultimately reveals to the landlord that the tenant to whom the property was let out has put some other person into possession of that property. In such a situation, it would be difficult for the landlord to prove, by direct evidence, the contract or agreement or understanding between the tenant and the sub­tenant.

It would also be difficult for the landlord to prove, by direct evidence, that the person to whom the property had been sub­let had paid monetary consideration to the tenant. Payment of rent, undoubtedly, is an essential element of lease or sub­lease. It may be paid in cash or in kind or may have been paid or promised to be paid. It may have been paid in lump sum in EC No:E­13/08/09, Raghunandan Saran Ashok Saran (HUF) Vs. National Insurance Co. Ltd.

advance covering the period for which the premises is let out or sub­let or it may have been paid or promised to be paid periodically. Since payment of rent or monetary consideration may have been made secretly, the law does not require such payment to be proved by affirmative evidence and the court is permitted to draw its own inference upon the facts of the case proved at the trial, including the delivery of exclusive possession to infer that the premises were sub­let."

As far as the plea taken by the legal heirs of the appellant that they being the legal heirs were entitled to inherit the tenancy after the death of the Respondent Sh. M.L.Sharma, is again of no consequence because in this case the allegation of subletting was made during the life time of the deceased appellant.

Merely because his legal heirs have now been brought on record to represent the estate of the said respondent, they cannot be considered as statutory tenant and in any case would not take away the mischief of subletting committed by the appellant in his life time.(see HARI CHAND (DECEASED) THRU LRS v. RAJENDER NATH & ORS RC. S.A. No. 16 /2002 Reserved On: 11.11.2010 Decided On:
15.WHETHER THE LANDLORD HAD WAIVED HIS RIGHT TO EC No:E­13/08/09, Raghunandan Saran Ashok Saran (HUF) Vs. National Insurance Co. Ltd.

SEEK EVICTION DUE TO LONG EXCLUSIVE POSSESSION OF THE R­2 TO R­4 (NO) Let me now revert to the question whether long exclusive possession of the respondents 2 to 4 in the premises would invite the court to hold that the landlord had waived the right to evict the tenant on the ground of subletting. An order of eviction can be passed under cite25†Section 14(1)(b) of the Act only if the ingredients enumerated herein earlier are satisfied. In order to prove subletting, it must be shown that the appellant Nos.

2 to 4 were inducted without the consent in writing of the landlord. It is now well settled that to constitute waiver of benefit conferred by provisions of the Act, conscious relinquishment of such benefit must be proved. In the case of Duli Chand (Dead) by LRs. vs.

Jagminder Dass [(1990) 1 SCC 169], the Hon'ble Supreme Court while dealing with a case of subletting and waiver on the part of the landlord, emphasized that the consent in writing of the landlord for subletting or parting with possession was essential under cite25†Section 14(1)(b) of the Act. The view expressed in the aforesaid decision was also the view in the case of cite27†Pulin Behari Lal vs.

Mahadeb Dutta and Ors. [(1993) 1 SCC 629] in which this Court reiterated the principle that in the absence of conscious relinquishment of right to eviction, the question of waiver on the ground EC No:E­13/08/09, Raghunandan Saran Ashok Saran (HUF) Vs. National Insurance Co. Ltd.

of subletting for eviction by the landlord did not arise at all. In the present case there is no conscious relinquishment. Therefore the mere knowledge vis­à­vis the employment of R­2 since 1952 would not mean that that the landlord had waived his right to seek eviction later.

In view of discussion made above, the petitioner has been able to establish his case under cite14†S.14(1)(b) of the DRC Act, 1958. The premises to be vacated by all the respondents. The eviction order is accordingly passed in favour of the petitioner and against the respondents with respect to the tenanted premises. File be consigned to record room. Announced in the open court on this 28th day of November, 2011.
